items.title: Fed Rate Hike in October Looks Less Likely After Weak Jobs Report
items.description: Trends Follow Us On Google Fed Rate Hike in October Looks Less Likely After Weak Jobs Report By Snejana Farberov October 2, 2026 David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images Coming off an unexpected surge in August , the U.S. labor market stumbled in September, adding just 29,000 new jobs as the unemployment rate edged up to 4.2%. According to the latest report from the Bureau of Labor Statistics , released Friday, economic recovery suffered a setback at the start of fall, with nonfarm payrolls growing by only about a third of economist expectations. These weaker-than-anticipated job numbers make it less likely that the Federal Reserve would opt for another interest rate hike when the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meets on Oct. 27-28. Just minutes after the release, CME FedWatch showed odds rising to 85% that the federal funds rate will hold steady at its current 3.75%-4% range, up from 75% a day ago. The trend was echoed by the prediction marketplace Kalshi . Work sectors that saw the strongest growth last month included health care, which added 17,000 new jobs, along with construction (+11,000 jobs), and manufacturing (+9,000). Meanwhile, financial activities employment continued to lag, shedding 7,000 jobs over the month and 129,000 since a recent peak in May 2025. July was revised down by 31,000 jobs, and the change for August was revised down by 29,000, from +162,000 to +133,000, adding up to 60,000 fewer payrolls than previously reported across the two months. Realtor.com® senior economist Jake Krimmel says that while the September numbers are a "clear miss," they mostly extend trends that have defined the market in recent years. "Layoffs haven’t picked up, and jobless claims have been falling , so the low hire, low fire market is likely to stay entrenched as we head into 2027," says Krimmel. What will the Federal Reserve do? For the Fed, the economist maintains that this latest print is unlikely to have a major impact on decision making around rate hikes this fall. "Despite tepid September job growth, unemployment remains low, so in short, this is no labor disaster that would pull the FOMC’s focus off inflation," notes Krimmel. The central bank, headed by Chairman Kevin Warsh , is intent on containing supply-driven inflation from geopolitical instability and higher energy prices. After the soft jobs report, a hold looks even more likely for October. However, the consensus remains that another hike will be coming before the end of the year, whch means that the pressure that sent the 10-year Treasury to a 24-year high and pushed Freddie Mac’s mortgage rate from 6.66% at the beginning to September to 7.28% this week has not gone away. Loading... What this means for homebuyers For consumers and the housing market, Krimmel says the squeeze continues at both ends, with a still- sluggish labor market on one side and financial conditions getting tougher on the other. The 62 basis point increase in mortgage rates in a span of a single month works out to about $19,000 less house on a $2,000 per month budget for principal and interest. That blow to housing affordability is reflected in September's housing data , with pending sales down 4.1% year over year, the largest drop since March 2025, and 20.8% of listings seeing a price cut, the highest single month of price cuts in nearly four years. "With a rather static jobs picture likely to persist this fall, buyers and sellers should not plan on a particularly dynamic housing market in the near term either," warns Krimmel. She has worked as a general assignment journalist in New York City and Long Island for 16 years, writing for New York Post, Daily Mail, and News 12. items.title: RealPage wins pause on New York’s algorithmic rent-setting ban
items.description: An article from Dive Brief RealPage wins pause on New York’s algorithmic rent-setting ban The federal court agreed to grant a preliminary injunction while it mulls the software maker’s claims that the state’s new law violates the First Amendment. Published Oct. 2, 2026 Julie Strupp Senior Editor Share Copy link Email LinkedIn X/Twitter Facebook Print License Add us on Google The Thurgood Marshall United States Courthouse, where the 2nd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals hears cases, in Manhattan in New York City, N.Y. Spencer Platt / Staff via Getty Images Listen to the article 3 min This audio is auto-generated. Please let us know if you have feedback . Dive Brief: RealPage has won a pause on New York’s recent algorithmic rent-pricing restrictions while the federal court mulls the real estate software provider’s argument that the new law violates the First Amendment, according to Sept. 29 filings in the U.S. District Court, Southern District of New York. The court also denied the state’s January request to dismiss the lawsuit. Last November, RealPage sued New York state on free speech grounds and asked for a preliminary injunction on its residential rent-pricing algorithm prohibition, which took effect in December 2025. RealPage claimed that the statute is overly broad and prohibits protected speech, namely, its algorithmic pricing advice, “by equating these recommendations with ‘an unlawful agreement,’” per the filing. RealPage told the court that without an injunction, the firm risked “self-censoring, penalties, and prosecution” for engaging in constitutionally protected speech, according to the filing. The court determined that “algorithmically-informed recommendations of housing prices — is commercial speech” and agreed to hold off on enforcement. Dive Insight: In October 2025, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul signed S.7882 , amending the state’s existing antitrust law to prohibit anyone from facilitating an agreement between residential rental property owners or managers “to not compete with respect to residential rental dwelling units, including by operating or licensing a software, data analytics service, or algorithmic device.” RealPage sued in response, arguing in its Nov. 26 complaint that the law represents a “sweeping and unconstitutional ban on lawful speech specifically intended to outlaw software developed and sold by companies like Plaintiff RealPage, Inc. that provide information and advice to owners and managers of rental properties.” The following month, it asked the court to pause enforcement while its case was heard. The court affirmed in the most recent filing that the crux of RealPage’s business model is the “communication of pricing information to its users,” and that New York’s law “expressly” regulates that communication. Historically, RealPage has generated rent pricing recommendations using a blend of private and public data, but it has mostly transitioned away from the former as part of a November 2025 settlement agreement with the Department of Justice in a separate case. New York is the first state to impose such a ban, but cities like Jersey City, New Jersey; Providence, Rhode Island; Philadelphia; Minneapolis; San Francisco; and Seattle have passed similar measures. items.title: Mortgage Banking Summit: ‘Street fight’ market concentrates growth toward nondelegated lenders
items.description: The competition for mortgage market share has become a “street fight,” with production and talent increasingly shifting toward the broker/nondelegated correspondent channel, industry executives said Thursday at HousingWire ’s Mortgage Banking Summit in Dallas. “We are absolutely, in my opinion, in a street fight,” Rich Weidel, CEO of Princeton Mortgage , said on stage. Citing data from RETR covering 2,070 lenders, Weidel noted that half of lenders saw net production shrinkage last year, while only 57 companies across all channels grew by more than $400 million over the past 12 months. That small cohort represented only 2.8% of companies, but they captured roughly two-thirds of all production growth in the market. With volumes plateauing and mortgage rates still elevated , Weidel said lenders are being sorted into two groups: capital winners and cost-to-produce winners. Capital-driven players are using their balance sheets to lure originators with upfront signing bonuses in an “acqui-hire” strategy, which only works if these producers can be retained. Cost-focused competitors are attacking their per-loan expenses so they can offer originators more compensation, better rates for consumers or both. “If you look at the data, there’s two camps: those [loan originators] that are moving toward the companies where they’re getting upfront signing bonuses,” Weidel said. “We’re also seeing them moving into the nondelegated channel ; the nondelegated starts to look like the green shoots that we’re seeing in traditional IMBs, the sort of brokers becoming non-dels and mortgage bankers getting really lean and mean. “There’s this crop of companies that are starting to operate in an entirely new cost structure, and we’re seeing the production move to that.” Production migration Rick Roque , senior vice president of retail growth and M A at NFM Lending, said RETR’s loan officer tracking data confirms the trend toward nondelegated models and away from traditional bank and independent mortgage bank ( IMB ) platforms. Between Jan. 1 and Sept. 9 of this year, 17,438 loan officers changed employers, moving about $6.8 billion in production. Independent mortgage bankers recorded a net loss of 97 loan officers and $1.8 billion in production over that period, while banks posted a net loss of 230 LOs and $5 billion in production. Brokers , by contrast, showed a net gain of 327 loan officers and $6.8 billion in production. Roque attributed much of that momentum to the appeal of the nondelegated correspondent channel, which allows teams to operate with a lender-like platform while shifting much of the fixed cost and operational risk to a larger counterparty. James Deitch, co-founder and CEO of Teraverde , described a hierarchy of costs, with banks typically having a higher cost structure than IMBs and brokers. Roque sees a correlation to this with the LO migration trends. “The nondelegated correspondent is a brilliant strategy because you can operate as a lender, especially given the advances in technology,” Roque said. “At NFM , we have large production teams who have dedicated underwriting, closing and funding out of corporate, while non-delegate correspondents, they’ve grown to a size where UWM has dedicated their underwriters, closers, and funders to that organization. “It’s an incredible strategy because you get all the benefits and all the execution without any of the cost.” Related More: Correspondent Lending Loan Officer Mortgage Banking Summit 2026

items.title: HECM originations sink to lowest level since 2020, HMBS issuance down 17% in September
items.description: September produced more declines in the market for federally insured reverse mortgages, with the number of Home Equity Conversion Mortgage ( HECM ) endorsements dropping 6.7% and HECM Mortgage-Backed Securities ( HMBS ) issuance down 17% from the prior month. The monthly HECM data published Thursday by Reverse Market Insight ( RMI ) showed that endorsements in September declined to 1,790 — down from 1,919 in August and the lowest total for any month since April 2020. RMI said in its report that case numbers, representing submitted applications for new HECM loans, were running “solidly” in the range of about 3,000 per month from May through July. But many of these applicants dropped out of lender pipelines, resulting in fewer closed-loan endorsements for the ensuing months. The top lenders for September were Finance of America (408 endorsements), Mutual of Omaha Mortgage (366), Longbridge Financial (342), Fairway Home Mortgage (65) and South River Mortgage (63). Through the first three quarters of the year, Finance of America (FOA) widened its lead with 3,838 endorsements. Mutual of Omaha (3,709), Longbridge (3,151), Goodlife (806) and South River (634) rounded out the top five. When comparing the first nine months of 2026 to the same period a year ago, Longbridge and South River saw marginal growth in endorsements of 1% and 5%, respectively, while the other top-five lenders saw declines ranging from 6% to 24%. The “Big 3” of FOA, Mutual of Omaha and Longbridge held a combined HECM market share of 59.1% through the first three quarters of the year, up from 55.9% during the same period in 2025. Further down the rankings, Movement Mortgage doubled its production from 17 loans in August to 35 in September, while Plaza Home Mortgage grew its endorsements from 28 to 41 during the month. In his weekly “Ribler on Rates” video series, Dan Ribler — vice president of capital markets and strategy at Longbridge — discussed the impacts of inflation and mortgage rates, which continue to serve as headwinds for all mortgage lenders. He noted that the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) index for August, released earlier this week, showed annual inflation of 3.4%, or 3% when excluding volatile food and energy prices. “We’re seeing the bond market respond with a bull steepener. The front end of the curve, we’re seeing yields come down, where 10-year yields are roughly flat,” Ribler said. “That makes perfect sense, because on the front end of the curve, cooler inflation data means there’s a lower probability that the Fed will hike rates next time they meet.” New View on HMBS issuance New View Advisors also released HMBS data for September on Thursday, based on its analysis of issuance from Ginnie Mae and private sources. It found that volume for last month totaled $446 million, down $91 million (-17%) from August. But there were 70 pools issued in September, up from 65 in August. FOA led all issuers in September at $175 million, although that was down from $257 million in August. Longbridge ($134 million) and Mutual of Omaha ($92 million) saw only marginal declines in volume during the month. First-participation pool production in September dropped to $266 million, down from $309 million in August and $313 million in September 2025. New View cautioned that “issuers will struggle to maintain this rate of production with the 10-year Treasury yield at its highest level since 2002.” Through the first three quarter of this year, FOA was No. 1 with $917 million in first-participation issuance. Longbridge was next at $790 million, followed by Mutual of Omaha ($546 million) and Onity Mortgage Corp. ($151 million). Onity, which completed a sale of reverse mortgage servicing rights to FOA over the summer, did not issue any first-participation pools in September. items.title: Carnegie Mellon's Ken Griffin-Backed Campus Has Miami Developers Salivating
items.description: Carnegie Mellon's Ken Griffin-Backed Campus Has Miami Developers Salivating October 2, 2026 | 6:49 pm ET Chloe Gallivan, South Florida When the news broke on Wednesday that billionaire Ken Griffin was spending $3B to bring a Carnegie Mellon University campus to Miami’s Wynwood neighborhood, commercial real estate professionals sprang into action. It took just a few hours for Wynwood-based Dwntwn Realty Advisors to send out an email blast marketing 17 of its nearby listings, ranging from development sites to office and retail space within walking distance of the planned campus. The response was immediate and enthusiastic. “Our website has been lighting up like a Christmas tree, and we're getting phone calls from all over,” Dwntwn Realty Managing Partner Devlin Marinoff said Thursday. He and his partner, Tony Arellano, “have been busy from morning to night since yesterday. I think it's only going to keep going.” Courtesy of Griffin Catalyst Carnegie Mellon University Miami expects to start enrolling students by 2028. The announcement that a top 20 national university was coming to Wynwood — a former industrial area known today for its massive graffiti murals, nightlife and recent building boom — has set off a frenzy of commercial real estate activity. Rilea Group, which is building two multifamily projects in Wynwood, has already set up a meeting to fly overseas partners to Miami next week to start discussing potential student housing projects, President Diego Ojeda said. “I would have never considered it before,” he told Bisnow . Griffin, the founder of hedge fund Citadel and the world's 33rd-richest person , spent $1.1B to acquire the roughly 35-acre Mana Wynwood convention center from Moishe Mana , one of Miami’s largest landowners, this week. He donated the land, and a few acres he already owned nearby, to the Pittsburgh-based school. The deal closed three years after Griffin’s people first approached Mana to buy the site for a college campus, Mana told Bisnow in a phone interview. At first, the Israel-born developer didn't want to sell so soon after he had just finished building the convention center, which hosts concerts, art fairs, productions, conventions and major events. But after spending a few days digesting the proposal, he brought Griffin's team back. “It’s going to change so many young people's lives and many people's lives over there, and it's going to strengthen Wynwood to make it more of a neighborhood, make it more of a cultural hub, this is for sure,” Mana said. “This was my original vision.” Mana had assembled the properties for between $50M and $70M, he said. By selling them for more than $1B — some of which he was paid a year and a half ago, he said — he is “passing the torch to Ken.” Griffin pledged a total of $3B to Carnegie Mellon, the largest-ever donation in American higher education, $2B of which is dedicated to building a campus on the site, with plans to start construction next year and begin enrollment by 2028. Carnegie Mellon University Miami’s curriculum will focus on human health and biological discovery, national security, energy and climate resilience, advanced manufacturing and industrial transformation, school officials said. Eventually, it is planned to house 3,500 undergraduate, master’s and Ph.D. students — a powerful pipeline of potential hires for companies in the area. “One of the primary things that drives activity and drives companies to an area is an accumulation of talent,” said Kevin Gonzalez , Colliers senior vice president and one of the leasing agents for The Gateway at Wynwood office building. “I can't think of a stronger concentration of talent than a Carnegie Mellon campus that is going to be fairly large,” he said. “That alone is going to really make that a primary focus for a lot of the corporate tenants.” Courtesy of Griffin Catalyst The neighborhood's office buildings have already attracted big-name companies like A

items.title: Federal Realty Spends $508M On Alabama Power Center
items.description: Federal Realty Spends $508M On Alabama Power Center October 2, 2026 | 1:46 pm ET Ciara Long, New York City A half-billion-dollar sale of a Birmingham, Alabama, shopping center shows that deep-pocketed investors are still hungry for retail. Google Maps The AMC movie theater at The Summit, an 870K SF mall in Birmingham, Alabama Maryland-based Federal Realty Investment Trust acquired The Summit, an open-air retail property spanning 870K SF, from its original developer for $508M, according to a release . The deal marks the first time the property, which is the state’s most-visited retail destination , has changed hands since Bayer Properties developed it more than 30 years ago. "Opportunities to buy truly irreplaceable, dominant assets like The Summit don't come along often, and we can't be more excited about adding this property to our portfolio," Federal Realty CEO and President Don Wood said in a statement. The Summit, which is 92% occupied, sits between Mountain Brook — one of the wealthiest suburbs in the U.S. — and Vestavia Hills, where median household incomes are almost double Alabama's statewide median . The acquisition deepens Federal Realty's holdings in the middle of the country after decades focused on retail and mixed-use developments on the coasts. The REIT's seven-property central region portfolio now spans 2.7M SF and includes properties in Chicago, Kansas City and Omaha. Federal Realty owns a total of 28.8M SF of commercial real estate across 103 properties. The REIT expects to fund its acquisition of The Summit via a combination of asset sales, cash flow and proceeds from recently issued debt . The deal for the Birmingham retail property also follows executives’ proclamations during a February earnings call that the REIT intends to buy more retail around the country over the course of 2026. Federal Realty boosted its earnings guidance at the end of the second quarter . Its shares are up more than 8% in 2026, although they had been rising faster in the first half of the year before the recent run-up in borrowing costs placed a damper on real estate stocks. Federal Realty’s acquisition comes as retail's post-pandemic recovery and historically low construction pipeline have caught the eye of investors. Roughly $33B of retail properties changed hands during the first six months of the year, up 14% year-over-year and the best first half since 2022, according to JLL . Rents have risen sharply in recent years, especially in the Sun Belt markets where construction has not kept pace with population growth, generating strong returns. “By far, our most favorite asset class over the past, probably, three years, four years has been retail,” Wafra Head of Real Estate David Hamm said Wednesday at Bisnow 's National Commercial Real Estate Finance Event in New York. “It's just been a phenomenal performer.” Continue reading this story with a free account Log in or register Contact Ciara Long at ciara.long@bisnow.com Related Topics: Don Wood , Federal Realty Investment Trust , Gen Z , Malls , Shopping Centers
